transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Tethys), Priya Rao (Tethys), Sara Kim (Tethys)

Summary (auto): quick SDK walkthrough for Redwood API, Console and Optimize tool; focus on Python/TypeScript quickstarts, auth options (API key vs S S O/Sam L), environment setup, and pilot next steps. Security and V P C questions surfaced.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, my name's Maya Chen, I'm the AE on the account and with me is Diego Ruiz, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Diego: hi all, excited to walk through the SDKs and a quick live demo of the python and typescript quickstarts. if at any point shout out questions.
[00:22] Liam: hey thanks, we're mainly curious about how fast we can get a dev to hit the API and also how auth and env setup looks in our tooling.
[00:28] Diego: great, so i'll share my screen — showing the repo — this is the redwood-sdk-quickstarts, there's a python folder and a ts folder. the python quickstart is a small sample that uses requests and the rwd-sdk client. note: internal name may be 'redwood-client' in some of our older docs.
[00:45] Diego: auth: we recommend API keys for dev & quickstarts, and S S O / Sam L integration for team accounts and enterprise. in the quickstart .env we demo REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_API_URL and optional REDWOOD_MODEL override for pinning models.
[01:10] Priya: on the S S O piece — we need SAML + SCIM provisioning, and K M S integration for keys. is that supported?
[01:18] Maya: yes, for Private and Dedicated customers we support SAML/SCIM and customer-managed K M S/H S M integrations. for hosted, we offer encrypted at rest and customer key options for enterprise tiers. i'll attach the security pack after the call.
[01:34] Diego: back to SDKs — python example: pip install redwood-sdk (note: package name sometimes differs in older repos), then set export REDWOOD_API_KEY=xxx, run python examples/quickstart.py to POST a generate request. the sample shows streaming and non-streaming responses.
[01:56] Diego: typescript side: npm i @redwood/inference (example), set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY in a .env, or use the SDK helper that reads env vars; we show both fetch-based and websocket streaming examples.
[02:15] Liam: quick question on latency — we saw some benchmarks in the deck; for our use case, mostly short prompts (~200 tokens) at 50 requests/sec, what would you recommend? hosted or dedicated?
[02:30] Diego: for 50 rps with tight p95 latency, dedicated or dedicated burst is recommended. hosted can work but you may see variability during peak if multitenant. also batching is a tradeoff — batching reduces cost but increases p95. Redwood Optimize recommends batching config per workload; we can run a small benchmark for you.
[02:55] Priya: about environment setup — we're on AWS, behind a corporate proxy, and our deploys are containerized. does the SDK need special network egress?
[03:06] Diego: no special ports, HTTPS outbound to the REDWOOD_API_URL. for private deployments we can do V P C peering or private endpoints. there is also an on-prem option if you need air-gapped.
[03:22] Sara: curious about the Console — the dev console you showed earlier, can we see token-level cost and per-route dashboards?
[03:29] Maya: yes, Console exposes per-route token breakdown, latencies, error rates and you can set SLO alerting. the Optimize tab gives active suggestions — e.g., quantized model recommendation or cache/prefix suggestions. sometimes it's labeled Redwood Opti-mize in older UI screenshots.
[03:44] Liam: on keys and rotation — do you support short-lived keys or role-based service principals?
[03:51] Diego: we support API keys with rotation via the Console and for enterprise you can integrate with your K M S to sign tokens, plus RBAC in the Console so service roles are possible. we'll include docs.
[04:05] Maya: i'm going to demo a live quickstart now — i'll run the python sample and create a generate call so you can see the full flow.
[04:12] Diego: note the sample uses prefix caching example — it's a small local cache to simulate KV cache behavior; in prod our runtime does KV cache automatically. sometimes transcripts show K V spelled out, sorry.
[04:30] Maya: running... ok request sent — response streaming — you can see tokens arriving.
[05:00] Liam: looks good. one thing: how do we pin model versions for rollouts? we need deterministic behavior during canary.
[05:10] Diego: you can pin model versions in the route config or via the API; Console supports canary and A/B rollout, and we have automatic fallback to a compatible variant if capacity is constrained.
[05:25] Priya: tell me more about cost controls — we need to keep predictability.
[05:30] Maya: pricing for hosted is usage-based; for Dedicated you can do reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits. Optimize gives recommendations to reduce token spend like suggest shorter contexts, batching, or a quantized model. we'll include sample numbers in the pricing sheet.
[05:48] Liam: security question — audit logs, retention, and data residency?
[05:53] Maya: we provide audit logs accessible in Console with export, retention options as an add-on, and Private deployments can be colocated in region for residency.
[06:07] Diego: jumping to the typescript quickstart — here's the sample code showing auth via env var and an example of function/tool calling; there's a small example of structured output parsing.
[06:26] Diego: note: some older code references 'tool calling' as plugin call, transcription may show different names.
[06:34] Liam: any gotchas for our CI/CD? we run ephemeral environments and would prefer not to bake long-lived keys into images.
[06:42] Diego: best practice: use short-lived keys from your vault or CI secrets manager, or use role-based service principals for deployments. we can show an example GitHub Action snippet that fetches a key at runtime.
[06:58] Priya: on private deployment — latency wise if we colocate in our V P C region, do you support autoscaling GPUs?
[07:06] Diego: yes, Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity, private on-prem can be configured with our orchestration, we can provide expected throughput per GPU type in the benchmark doc.
[07:22] Liam: can you run a quick benchmark with our sample payloads?
[07:26] Maya: yes, next step is to run a small benchmark — Diego will coordinate.
[07:33] Diego: i'll ask you to share a sample of typical prompts and target p95 and throughput; we can run the benchmark on hosted first, then replicates on a dedicated config if you want.
[07:45] Priya: regarding compliance, do you have SOC2 report and ISO certs?
[07:49] Maya: yes, we will send SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestation in the security pack.
[07:55] Sara: dev experience question — are there language-specific helpers for prompt templates?
[08:00] Diego: both SDKs expose a prompt template helper and a response parser; in TS we show a helper that returns typed outputs via zod schema in the example repo.
[08:12] Liam: on embeddings — not our primary focus but might be later — do the SDKs support embeddings and reranking?
[08:18] Diego: yes, the API supports text-generation, chat, embeddings, and reranking; quickstarts include a small embeddings example as well.
[08:28] Priya: what about rate limits for the hosted API?
[08:32] Maya: default quotas apply to free tiers; paid tiers can increase limits and we support rate-limit headers so you can backoff gracefully.
[08:40] Diego: switching back, showing the Quickstart README — it includes a sample .env.example, runbook for streaming with websockets, and a troubleshooting section with common proxy errors.
[08:55] Liam: proxy errors have bitten us before — do you have sample env for corporate proxy?
[09:00] Diego: yes, we have a snippet that sets HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY for local dev. we'll include that in the repo.
[09:10] Maya: i'm going to open the Console to show route config — here you can set model, token limits, rollout policy, and enable Optimize suggestions and caching.
[09:24] Diego: in Console you can also set RBAC roles for team members and configure API key rotation.
[09:30] Priya: for pilot we'll likely start hosted with a fixed monthly spend cap, and if it looks good move to Dedicated.
[09:37] Maya: perfect that's a common path. we'll propose a pilot plan in the pricing sheet.
[09:44] Liam: any warnings about behavior drift when switching models/quantized variants?
[09:50] Diego: yes, switching models can change outputs. we recommend running regression tests and evals with your prompt sets; Console can tie regression alerts to prompt sets/evals.
[10:05] Priya: can we automate evals?
[10:08] Diego: yes, you can run evals as part of CI using our eval API; we'll share an example.
[10:15] Maya: quick note: we maintain a model catalog with verified performance profiles — that helps pick quantized variants for cost vs quality.
[10:26] Liam: are there built-in retry/fallbacks on the client?
[10:29] Diego: SDK has retry helpers and automatic fallback policies can be set at routing layer.
[10:35] Maya: ok moving toward wrap-up, i'll summarize next steps.
[10:41] Maya: Redwood items: send quickstart repo links (py + ts), security pack (SOC2/ISO/KMS notes), pricing/pilot proposal; Tethys items: share sample prompts, desired SLOs and confirmation on pilot cap.
[10:58] Liam: timeline — we can confirm pilot scope by next week and go live with benchmarks the week after.
[11:05] Maya: great. Diego, anything to add?
[11:08] Diego: i'll follow up with a short runbook for the benchmark and a GH Action example for ephemeral secrets.
[11:15] Priya: thanks, this was useful. we'll look at the repo and reply with our sample payloads.
[11:21] Sara: thanks all.

[11:30] (end of recording)

Notes:
- Links shared during call: Quickstart repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstarts), Security pack doc (drive link placeholder), Pricing sheet (sheets link placeholder).
- Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions: 'Sam L' = SAML, 'K V cache' = KV cache, 'Redwood Opti-mize' = Redwood Optimize.

Recap (auto): Demo covered SDK install + quickstarts for Python and TypeScript, auth options (API key vs SAML/SSO), env config (.env examples, HTTPS_PROXY), Console features (route pinning, rollout, RBAC, logs), Optimize suggestions and benchmarking next steps. Agreed next steps: repo and security docs to be shared, Tethys to confirm pilot scope and sample prompts.
